chapter_theme: Guided by the ascetic, Kovalan and Kannaki travel the Pandya land by night trusting its fame for safety; in a Brahmin village Kovalan meets Kausikan with Madhavi's letter, clears her and owns the fault as his own, sends the letter on to his parents, and with bards on the road comes by breeze, dawn sounds and the Vaigai to Madurai, where river, flowers and flags grieve and warn as if they knew what is coming, and the couple enter the outer settlement of the virtuous.

cast.role: son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband, travelling to Madurai
the woman ascetic who guides the couple to Madurai; in this kaathai named only by epithets (புண்ணிய முதல்வி, மாதவத்தாட்டி, அறவி)
a Brahmin youth of Puhar, Madhavi's messenger, who finds Kovalan on the road
the dancer and courtesan of Puhar whom Kovalan left
Kovalan's father, the wealthy merchant of Puhar
Kovalan's mother, the mistress of the great house
wandering bards met on the road to Madurai
the Earth, personified as a woman
the moon, named as the founder of the Pandya line
the river Vaigai of Madurai, personified as a woman

silappathikaram:13:1-10.reading: After the forest guise has been put off, someone at the holy lady's feet reasons that this young woman cannot bear the fierce summer sun and her small feet have never trodden the hot pebbled forest, and that the fame has spread everywhere of the land guarded by the Pandyas of the straight sceptre, where the bear does not dig the anthill, the tiger does not attack the deer, and serpent, demon, crocodile and thunder do no harm to those who depend on it.
silappathikaram:13:1-10.nuance: The safety of the road is given as reputation (இசை, line 10), heard of rather than seen, and it reaches past men to beasts, demons and thunder. The text does not name the speaker: the deliberation runs into the next unit and ends with குரவரும் நேர்ந்த (line 14), the elder's consent, so it is most likely Kovalan proposing night travel to the ascetic. The praise of the Pandya's straight sceptre is set on the threshold of the realm where the Pandya will kill Kovalan without inquiry.
silappathikaram:13:1-10.event: On the road to Madurai the travellers weigh the summer heat against the safety of the Pandya's land before going on.

claims.claim: in the land of a king whose sceptre is straight, even wild beasts, demons and thunder do no harm to those who rely on it

silappathikaram:13:11-28.reading: Since the moonlight protects living beings better than daylight and there is no danger in passing the long road by night, the elder agrees, and the travellers, who wait for the hour of sunset like the subjects of a cruel king, see the moon, the founder of the Pandya line, rise with its host of stars spreading milk-white rays, while the Earth asks the summer moon, with the southern breeze born on Malaya and grown in Madurai, to pour its white light on the young woman whom no star-garland, sandal paste, flower garland or leaf-chaplet now touches.
silappathikaram:13:11-28.nuance: The sun is likened to a cruel king whose subjects wait for him to set (line 15), and the moon that brings relief is the Pandya's own ancestor (line 18): the image of a bad reign and a protecting lineage are set side by side in the passage that admits the travellers to the Pandya land. The Earth's request (lines 19-28) is spoken before she is named in the next unit (பார்மகள், line 29); that the 'doll' (பாவை) is Kannaki, unadorned in her exile, is my reading.
silappathikaram:13:11-28.event: With the elder's consent the travellers wait for sunset and set out by night as the moon rises.

silappathikaram:13:29-50.reading: When the Earth has sighed and grown still, Kovalan, seeing his wife toil on the hard road, gives her his shoulder for her bangled hand and bids her not fear the roaming tiger, the calling owl and the growling bear; having heard the ascetic's teaching of dharma, free of harsh words, they pass the road, and at cock-crow reach a village of thread-wearing Brahmins versed in the Vedas, where he leaves his wife with the ascetic in a safe enclosure and goes beyond the thorn fence for water, sighing like a smith's bellows that he has brought her into the forest, so changed by grief that Kausikan does not know him.
silappathikaram:13:29-50.nuance: The bellows simile (ஊதுலைக் குருகின், line 45) gives Kovalan's grief a cause he owns: he is pained that his wife has come with him into the forest (line 44). The ascetic's teaching is described only as அறவுரை free of the speech of violence (மறவுரை நீத்த, line 34); its content is not given. The last three lines begin Kausikan's address to a creeper, which the next unit completes.
silappathikaram:13:29-50.event: Kovalan leads Kannaki through the night forest to a Brahmin village, leaves her with the ascetic and goes for water, unrecognised by Kausikan.

silappathikaram:13:51-75.reading: Resting in the shade of a green-leaved kurukkatthi arbour, Kausikan addresses the creeper as Madhavi, saying it suffers in the harsh summer with its flowers shed like Madhavi of the long eyes when Kovalan left her; Kovalan asks what he means, and Kausikan, saying he has found him unharmed, tells how Kovalan's father and mother became like serpents that had lost their gem, the kin fell into a sea of grief like a body without life, servants went everywhere to seek him, the great city was bewildered like Ayodhya when the hero left for the forest, and Madhavi, hearing from Vasanthamaalai, grew pale and fell on her couch, and when he went to her in her grief she wrote with her own hand, worshipping Kovalan's feet and asking him to end her sorrow, bidding Kausikan show it to him.
silappathikaram:13:51-75.nuance: Kausikan's speech to the creeper is a ruse of purpose (கொள்கையின் உரைப்போன், line 56): the creeper's name is the courtesan's, and the word Madhavi draws out the man he cannot recognise. The Ayodhya simile (lines 63-66) sets Puhar's loss of one merchant's son beside the city that lost Rama; the sense of அரசே தஞ்சம் (line 64) in the simile is not clear to me. Kovalan's family and Madhavi grieve in one report, the household and the courtesan side by side.
silappathikaram:13:51-75.event: Kausikan, sent from Puhar, recognises Kovalan and tells him of his parents' grief, the city's search and Madhavi's collapse and letter.

silappathikaram:13:76-92.reading: Kausikan says Madhavi gave him the clay-sealed letter and that he has wandered the roads and lands with it, and when he holds it out, Kovalan, knowing by the scent of the oil from her curled hair pressed into the clay seal the fragrance she spoke of when they lived together, cannot let it go, opens it and reads: she falls at his feet and asks him to take her guileless words to heart, she does not know her fault that made him leave by night with his high-born wife, against the service owed to his elders, and she asks him to remove the confusion of her helpless heart, hailing him as one of flawless sight.
silappathikaram:13:76-92.nuance: The letter names his elders' claim (குரவர்பணி, line 89) and his wife's birth (குலப்பிறப் பாட்டியொடு, lines 89-90), and asks for no return: it only asks what her fault was. The letter is the courtesan's speech in her own hand; the narrator voices the frame. தீத்திறம் புரிந்தோன் (line 78) I read as Kausikan naming himself as a Brahmin who keeps the sacred fire; it could refer to someone else.
silappathikaram:13:76-92.event: Kausikan hands Kovalan Madhavi's letter, which he knows by the scent of her hair on the seal, and he reads her plea.
silappathikaram:13:76-92.unit_note: Adjusted: the boundary at line 89/90 split the word குலப்பிறப்பாட்டியொடு (பாட்டியோ / டிரவிடை) and the letter's sentence; the end was moved from line 89 to line 92, where the letter closes with போற்றி.

silappathikaram:13:93-114.reading: Understanding the words she wrote, Kovalan decides she is without fault, his weariness leaves him, and seeing that the fault was his own, he says the letter's sense fits as well for his parents, bids Kausikan show it to them with his worship of their feet and sends him off to relieve their distress; then he returns to the ascetic, who sits with his wife of spotless chastity, joins a group of bards who sing the dance of the goddess, tunes the yazh with them and hears the paalai melody of the goddess of the leaping deer, and, singing along, asks them how far it is to Koodal.
silappathikaram:13:93-114.nuance: This is the one place in the journey where Kovalan names the cause of his ruin as his own fault (என்தீது, line 95), and he does it in answer to the courtesan, whom he clears (தன்றீ திலள், line 94). Later Kannaki tells the king that ஊழ்வினை drove him to Madurai (kaathai 20, line 69). The same letter, sent on to his parents, serves as his own plea to them. The musical lines (106-112) are technical and I have not tried to fix their terms.
silappathikaram:13:93-114.event: Kovalan, reading Madhavi's letter, holds her blameless and himself at fault, sends it on to his parents by Kausikan, and joins wandering bards on the road, asking them the distance to Madurai.
silappathikaram:13:93-114.unit_note: Adjusted: the start was moved from line 90 to line 93 so that the letter (lines 87-92) stays whole; line 92 ends it and line 93 (என்றவள் எழுதிய) begins Kovalan's response.

silappathikaram:13:115-134.reading: The bards answer that the Madurai breeze has come here, unlike the Pothiyil breeze of the poets' tongues: it carries the smells of eaglewood and sandal paste, saffron, civet and musk, the flowers of the houses, the smoke of kitchens and of the cake-sellers' sweets, the incense men and women burn in the mansions and the smoke of the fire offerings, mingled with the fragrance of the Pandya's palace, so his prosperous old city is not far off, and even if they go alone none will stop them.
silappathikaram:13:115-134.nuance: Madurai is first reached by smell, and the city's breath mixes the kitchens, the merchants, the lovers' incense and the sacrificial fire with the king's own palace. The breeze itself is the Pandya land's (lines 25-26 of this kaathai already sent it from Malaya through Madurai). The closing assurance of safety for the lone traveller (line 134) repeats the opening fame of the Pandya's road.

silappathikaram:13:135-150.reading: With the ascetic as before they travel on in the dark, and the uproar of Koodal, loud as the dark sea, comes out to meet them and ends their sorrow: the morning drums of the great temple of the fierce god and of the king's palace, the chant of the Brahmins of the four Vedas, the recitation of the ascetics, the day drum of the warriors in the king's honour, the trumpeting of elephants taken in war and in pits, the neighing of horses in their stalls and the dawn songs of the kinai bards.
silappathikaram:13:135-150.nuance: The city's dawn is heard, not seen, from outside the walls, and it heals the travellers' grief (ஆரஞர் நீங்கி, line 150). The catalogue sets the temple and the palace side by side and the Brahmins' chant beside the ascetics' (மாதவர், line 142), and several items, the stalled horse (பணைநிலைப் புரவி, line 147) and the captured elephants, are those of the Sangam Madurai dawn in Maduraikkanchi.
silappathikaram:13:135-150.event: Travelling on by night, the three hear Madurai's dawn sounds and their grief lifts.
silappathikaram:13:135-150.unit_note: Adjusted: the end was moved from line 151 to line 150; line 150 (ஆரஞர் நீங்கி) closes the dawn catalogue, and line 151 begins the list of flowers that dress the Vaigai.

silappathikaram:13:151-175.reading: The Vaigai is drawn as a woman whose banks of kuravam, vakulam, kongu, vengai and many other flowering trees are her girdle, whose sand heaps are her hips, whose flowered islet is her breasts, whose fallen kavir petals her red mouth, mullai her smile, carp her long eyes and dark water her flowered hair, the never-failing creeper of the Pandya clan, of high conduct that feeds the world, who, as if she knew what was to befall the young wife, wraps herself in a garment of holy fragrant flowers and hides her eye-filling flood, so that the woman of the swan's gait and her lord worship her, saying this is not a river of water but a river of flowers.
silappathikaram:13:151-175.nuance: The river's flowers, which the travellers read as beauty and worship, are given by the narrator as a veil over her tears (கண்ணிறை நெடுநீர் கரந்தனள், line 173): she knows the wife's fate and hides it. 'Never-failing' (பொய்யா, line 170) and 'feeds the world' are the Pandya river's old praise, and the poet names it as the poets' Vaigai (புலவர் நாவிற் பொருந்திய, line 169). Only the reader is told the river's grief; the couple see a river of flowers.
silappathikaram:13:151-175.event: The travellers reach the Vaigai, covered in flowers, and worship it as a river of flowers.
silappathikaram:13:151-175.unit_note: Adjusted: the start was moved from line 152 to line 151, where the flower list begins, and the end from line 174 to line 175, since the river's sentence (என, line 174) closes with the couple's worship (தொழுது, line 175).

silappathikaram:13:176-196.reading: Passing by the great ford where boats with horse, elephant and lion faces ply, they cross with the ascetic on a log raft to the flowering southern bank, and, judging it fitting to go round Madurai where the gods dwell, they skirt the moat girded with guard forest, where the blue lily, white lily and lotus, as if they knew for certain the lone sorrow that would come to the wife and her husband, weep and tremble with humming bees, and the long war-flags on the fort wave back as if saying 'do not come', and through fields, groves, tanks, lakes and gardens of coconut, plantain, areca and bamboo they enter the outer settlement of the old city where only those devoted to dharma dwell.
silappathikaram:13:176-196.nuance: Two omens are given as the narrator's 'as if' (போல, lines 186 and 190): the moat's flowers weep and the fort's flags wave the couple away. Both say plainly what the Vaigai's flowers hid. The couple avoid the royal ferry for a humble raft, and their first lodging in Madurai is the outer quarter of those devoted to dharma (lines 195-196), outside the walls where the king's justice will fail them.
silappathikaram:13:176-196.unit_note: Adjusted: the start was moved from line 175 to line 176, because the couple's worship on line 175 (தொழுது) closes the river's sentence and line 176 begins the crossing.
silappathikaram:13:176-196.event: The three cross the Vaigai on a raft, skirt Madurai's moat past weeping flowers and waving flags, and enter the city's outer settlement.

links.note: On entering the Pandya land the travellers rely on the fame that the Pandya's straight sceptre keeps even beasts and thunder from harming those who depend on it; in the court the same Pandya, having killed Kovalan, finds himself the thief and his sceptre bent.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the epic letting the travellers stake their lives on a king's reputation for protection and then making that king's failure fall on exactly the stranger who trusted it, so the praise of the sceptre at the border is the premise his own verdict on himself overturns.

links.note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by right; the epic's fame says that in the just Pandya's land even beasts, serpents and thunder spare those who depend on it.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show the claim that nature answers a just sceptre turning, in the epic, into a traveller's reason to trust a stranger king, a reputation the story then puts to the test with the travellers' own lives.

gains.a: the border praise gains its doctrinal ground: the fame rests on the Kural's teaching that a just reign orders nature itself
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its promise is taken as a guarantee by outsiders and so becomes something a king can betray

links.note: The couplet likens a king's lack of kindness to the world's lack of rain; the epic likens travellers waiting out the scorching sun to subjects waiting for a cruel king to set.
links.teaches: The Kural pictures the bad king through the weather and the epic pictures the weather through the bad king, so the pair shows the image of misrule running both ways, and the epic placing it, unprompted, at the first step into the Pandya's land.

gains.a: the simile gains the couplet's moral weight: the cruel king is a drought to all that lives, not just a passing discomfort
gains.b: the couplet gains a hope its subjects do not voice: that a cruel reign, like a summer day, has an end to wait for

links.note: On the road Kovalan, reading Madhavi's letter, says the fault was his own; before the king, Kannaki says ஊழ்வினை drove him to Madurai.
links.teaches: The pair shows the epic giving Kovalan's ruin two causes in two voices: his own confession of fault, made privately to clear the courtesan, and his wife's public appeal to former deeds, made to indict the king, so neither account stands alone as the poem's verdict.

links.note: The couplet says the sweet words of women who seek a man's wealth and not his love bring him harm; here a courtesan writes to a man who has lost his wealth, asking only what her fault was, and he judges her blameless and himself at fault.
links.teaches: The pair sets the Kural's rule that a courtesan's sweet words are for wealth against a courtesan's letter written after the wealth is gone, so the epic tests the rule on the one case it cannot explain and has the man himself withdraw the charge.

gains.a: Kovalan's verdict that Madhavi is faultless gains force from the rule it overturns: he clears her against the expected judgment of her class
gains.b: the couplet gains its limit case, a courtesan whose plea comes when the man has nothing left to give

links.note: Maduraikkanchi's dawn in Madurai has the Brahmins chanting the Veda, the elephants fed and the horses in their stalls (பணைநிலைப் புரவி); the epic's travellers hear the same dawn, the Vedic chant and the stalled horses' neighing among it, from outside the walls.
links.teaches: The epic reuses the Sangam catalogue of Madurai's dawn, phrase for phrase in places, but moves its hearer from the king the idyll counsels on impermanence to the strangers whom the city will destroy, so the idyll's warning that such splendour passes is carried out on the city itself.

gains.a: the catalogue gains its pedigree: Madurai's dawn is a set piece of the Sangam city, heard in the epic as the city's settled glory
gains.b: the idyll's counsel that wealth and splendour do not last gains a story in which this very Madurai, with its stalled horses and chanting Brahmins, is burned

links.note: The Paripadal fragment asks whether Madurai's fame can ever prove false as long as the Vaigai flows; the epic calls the Vaigai the never-failing (பொய்யா) creeper of the clan and has her hide her tears for the wife the city will wrong.
links.teaches: The Paripadal makes the flowing Vaigai the pledge that Madurai's fame cannot fail; the epic keeps the river unfailing but makes her the first to know that the city's justice will fail, so the pledge passes from the city to the river alone.

gains.a: the epic's 'never-failing' river gains the old pledge it echoes, which shows what the river's hidden grief is a grief for
gains.b: the fragment's confidence gains a story that separates the river's constancy from the city's fame

links.note: The Vaigai hides tears as if knowing the young wife's fate; in the court the king, called the lord of the Vaigai, loses his life at the hearing of her words.
links.teaches: The pair shows the river grieving at the entry for the wife and the river's lord dying at her word in the court, so the Vaigai frames Madurai's story from the woman's arrival to the king's death, siding with her in silence before he hears her.

links.note: At the moat the flowers weep and the flags wave as if saying 'do not come'; in the palace the queen dreams of the umbrella and sceptre falling and the gate bell shaking.
links.teaches: The pair shows the epic sending warnings to both sides of the coming wrong, to the strangers at the walls and to the queen in the palace, and having neither heeded, so the catastrophe is foreseen in nature and in sleep yet still unfolds.

source_issues: Lines 89-90: the word குலப்பிறப்பாட்டியொடு is split across the line end (பாட்டியோ / டிரவிடை), and the cut between units 76-89 and 90-114 fell inside it; the boundary was moved to line 92.
Lineation: the kaathai has 196 lines as shown but the edition's printed last line is 195, so the printed numbering is one short somewhere.
Lines 106-112: the technical terms of tuning the yazh (திவவு, உழை முதல் கைக்கிளை இறுவாய், மூவகைத் தானத்து) are taken as written; their sense was not checked against any source.
